---
title: "The feature pipeline"
---

What happens between raw voltage and a row in a feature table, and why the steps are
arranged the way they are.

## The path

```text
   your recording
        │
        │  a calculator normalises the source
        ▼
   raw AP / LF arrays  (n_channels, n_samples), volts  +  geometry  +  channel labels
        │
        │  destripe_ap_lf  —  the single shared destriping primitive
        ▼
   destriped AP / LF
        │
        │  features.lf / .csd / .ap / .spikes
        ▼
   per-snippet feature tables      <feature>_features.pqt
        │
        │  aggregation             median across snippets
        ▼
   raw_ephys_features.pqt
        │
        │  denoising               per-probe outlier suppression + transforms
        │  waveform remap          raw waveform columns -> spike-shape columns
        ▼
   raw_ephys_features_denoised.pqt        ← what models consume
```

## One source interface, many formats

The first design decision: **normalise the source, then share everything downstream.**

Every calculator subclasses `BaseFeatureCalculator` and implements only how to obtain raw
arrays and channel metadata. Once a recording is `(n_channels, n_samples)` in volts plus a
geometry dict, nothing further cares whether it came from SpikeGLX, NWB, Zarr, an lfpack
archive or an array in memory.

```text
BaseFeatureCalculator                      abstract source interface + compute_snippet
├── SpikeGlxLikeFeatureCalculator          shared spikeglx.Reader contract
│   ├── SpikeGLXFileFeatureCalculator      local AP/LF .bin/.cbin
│   └── IBLPIDFeatureCalculator            IBL insertion via ONE
├── SpikeInterfaceFeatureCalculator        shared SI BaseRecording contract
│   ├── NwbFeatureCalculator               NWB: local, streamed, DANDI
│   └── SpikeInterfaceZarrFeatureCalculator SI-native Zarr
├── LFPackFeatureCalculator                LF only: an lfpack archive
└── NumpyArrayFeatureCalculator            LF only: an array in memory
```

The two intermediate classes exist because reader-contract logic — reading a snippet,
filling geometry defaults, resolving channel labels — is identical within each family and
would otherwise be duplicated per source.

This is why supporting a new format is small: implement `_open_reader` or
`_open_recording` and the entire feature stack comes for free. A source with no reader to
share implements `load_raw_snippet` directly, as the two LF-only calculators do. Every
calculator also inherits `compute_denoised_features`, the
[multi-snippet route](#snippets-and-why-several).

### Composition for the acquisition axis

`NwbFeatureCalculator` faces a second problem: an NWB recording varies by backend (HDF5 or
Zarr) **and** by location (local, URL, DANDI). Four combinations, and subclassing would
give four classes.

Instead both axes are fields on one value object, `NwbSource`, and the calculator holds one
source per band. The combinatorial axis became data instead of types.

## Destriping is shared with the debug path

Neuropixels raw voltage carries structured artefacts — common-mode noise, per-channel
offsets, ADC striping. Destriping removes them before any feature is computed.

`destripe_ap_lf` delegates to `ibldsp.voltage.destripe` (AP) and
`ibldsp.voltage.destripe_lfp` (LF). It is deliberately the **single source of truth**: both
`compute_features_from_raw` and `get_destriped_snippet` call it.

That matters more than it sounds. `get_destriped_snippet` is the inspection path — what you
use to check whether destriping is behaving. If it had its own copy of the logic, it could
drift from the production path and you would be debugging a different pipeline than the one
producing your features.

Bad channels are handled here rather than dropped. `channel_labels` marks each channel
good, dead, noisy, or outside the brain, and destriping interpolates over the bad ones. The
labels then travel forward as a feature column, so a model can learn to distrust them
rather than having to guess.

LF that arrives already preprocessed — an lfpack archive, a decimated array — skips this
step with `FeatureComputationOptions(skip_lf_destripe=True)`: destriping it again at
its decimated sample rate would fail. With destriping skipped, the channel labels come
from the source's channel table instead.

## Feature families, and why they are separate

Four families, computed independently:

| family | band | measures |
|---|---|---|
| `lf` | LF | Band power, RMS, spectral decay |
| `csd` | LF | The same, on the current-source density and the bipolar reference |
| `ap` | AP | AP-band RMS, channel cross-correlation |
| `waveforms` | AP | Spike detection and waveform shape |

They are separate because their costs differ by orders of magnitude. `lf` and `csd` are
spectral estimates on a decimated signal — seconds. `waveforms` runs DARTsort spike
detection over the AP band — minutes to hours, and a heavy dependency tree that only ships
in the `[full]` extra.

Being separable means you can compute the cheap families on everything and the expensive
ones only where needed. It is also why each family writes its own
`<family>_features.pqt`: `skip_saved_computation` can then reuse a completed family and
recompute only what is missing, making a long run resumable.

### Why CSD as well as LF

The LFP at a channel is a mixture of activity from a wide radius — volume conduction is
not local. The current-source density, a spatial second derivative across channels, is far
more local, so `psd_delta` and `psd_delta_csd` carry genuinely different information about
the same signal. Both go in, and the decoder uses both. The `*_bpr` columns sit in between:
the first spatial difference, a bipolar reference between neighbouring contacts.

Spatial derivatives amplify noise, so the LF is Cadzow-denoised first. The parameters
depend on the layout (`features.cadzow_lfp_kwargs`): the NP1 checkerboard is filled onto
its full lateral × depth grid, which removes the seams the spatial windows used to leave
in the CSD, while NP2 contacts already fill theirs.

## Snippets, and why several

A snippet is one time window. The `SnippetWindow` defaults — `duration_ap=5.0`,
`duration_lf=25.0` — encode a real asymmetry: LF features need a long window to resolve
low-frequency power, while AP features are expensive and converge quickly.

But per-channel estimates from a single window are noisy. Compute several windows spread
through the recording and take their median, and the estimates stabilise. This is what
the training data did, which is why matching it matters for inference.

`calc.compute_denoised_features(n_snippets=...)` does exactly that in one call. It leaves
out the first and last 5 minutes, draws one start time (in whole seconds) in each of
`n_snippets` equal stretches of the rest, computes every snippet, then aggregates and
denoises. `get_snippet_start_times` and
`compute_aggregated_features` expose the two halves, to choose the windows yourself.

The output layout follows from that. The snippet directory name encodes `t_start`,
`duration_ap` and `duration_lf`, so windows over the same recording sit side by side and
never collide:

```text
<name>/
├── channels.pqt                                    per-probe, written once
├── probe_<name>_000300.0_01.0_01.0/
└── probe_<name>_000900.0_01.0_01.0/
```

`channels.pqt` sits at the probe level because geometry and anatomy are properties of the
insertion, not of a time window.

## Merging on physical position, not channel number

Channel metadata is merged onto the feature table on the **physical recording site** —
`(axial_um, lateral_um, shank)`, rounded to the nearest micrometre — not on the channel
index.

Version 0.7.0 changed this deliberately. Channel numbering is unreliable across data
sources: `rawInd`, the SpikeGLX index and the SpikeInterface index do not agree in general,
so joining on a channel number can silently mis-assign anatomy to features. Physical
position is unambiguous. `rawInd` is still carried, as descriptive metadata only.

## One shank per calculator

Feature computation assumes **all channels of a calculator are on one shank**. Several
steps work on the `x` / `y` positions (or the channel order) alone, and on a multi-shank
probe those do not tell the shanks apart: `x` is measured *within* each shank. On a
four-shank Neuropixels 2.0 probe (NP2.4), all four shanks report the same `x` (27–59 µm)
and the same columns, so the 384 channels sit on only 96 distinct `(x, y)` positions.

| step | uses | on a multi-shank probe |
|---|---|---|
| Destriping (`ibldsp` `destripe`, `destripe_lfp`) | `geometry["shank"]` | Shank-aware: CAR and the k-filter run per shank. Bad-channel interpolation uses `x` / `y` only |
| Channel metadata merge | `(axial_um, lateral_um, shank)` | Shank-aware |
| `lf` family | each channel alone | Unaffected beyond destriping |
| `csd` family (Cadzow, then `current_source_density`) | `x` / `y`, `col`, `row` | On a synthetic four-shank recording the default **raises** `ZeroDivisionError` in `ibldsp.cadzow.cadzow_denoiser`. With `CsdParams(denoise=False)` the zero spacing between shanks gives NaN, and the schema check raises `SchemaError`. Only with `scale=False` as well does it run, and then channels of different shanks at the same depth are differenced against each other |
| `cor_ratio` in the `ap` family (`xcor_acor_ratio`) | the 8 neighbouring channel numbers either side | Neighbours can lie on another shank — no error |
| `waveforms` (DARTsort) | `x` / `y` only | The shanks overlap in DARTsort's view of the probe, so detection neighbourhoods and spike localisation mix them — no check |
| Denoising at aggregation (`EphysDenoiser`) | `(lateral_um, axial_um)` | Every shank is put on one grid and filtered as a single surface — no error |

Only the NWB and Zarr calculators check. A recording whose SpikeInterface channel groups
span more than one shank raises:

```text
NotImplementedError: <name>: recording spans 4 shanks/groups ([0, 1, 2, 3]); per-shank
feature computation is not implemented yet. Pass a single shank's channels per calculator
(one ElectricalSeries per shank, or a per-shank channel subset).
```

The SpikeGLX and IBL PID calculators do not check, and the LFPack and NumPy calculators
set `shank` to 0 when the geometry has none.

So compute one shank at a time. For the LF families, slice each shank's channels and
geometry into its own `NumpyArrayFeatureCalculator`; each shank then gets its own `pid`
and a correct `shank` column:

```python
import numpy as np
import neuropixel

from ephysatlas.feature_calculators import (
    FeatureComputationOptions,
    NumpyArrayFeatureCalculator,
    SnippetWindow,
)

h = neuropixel.trace_header(version=2, nshank=4)   # or your recording's geometry
# lf: (384, n_samples) LF in volts, at its native rate fs_lf

for shank in np.unique(h["shank"]):
    sel = h["shank"] == shank
    calc = NumpyArrayFeatureCalculator(
        lf=lf[sel],
        fs_lf=fs_lf,
        geometry={key: np.asarray(value)[sel] for key, value in h.items()},
        name=f"my_probe_shank{int(shank)}",
    )
    result = calc.compute_snippet(
        SnippetWindow(t_start=0.0, duration_ap=1.0, duration_lf=25.0),
        FeatureComputationOptions(features_to_compute=["lf", "csd"], include_trajectory=False),
    )
```

On the same synthetic four-shank recording, each shank computed this way gets the NP2
Cadzow defaults and gives finite `lf` and `csd` features. There is no per-shank route yet for the AP families (`ap`,
`waveforms`) from a SpikeGLX file.

## Aggregation and denoising

Three steps, all per-probe.

**Aggregation** reduces the per-snippet tables to one row per `(pid, channel)`: the median
of each feature across snippets, except `spike_count`, whose mean counts a snippet with no
spikes as zero.

**Denoising** is two operations in sequence, `EphysTransformer` then `EphysDenoiser`:

1. **Transform.** Features whose schema declares one are transformed first — `rms_ap` and
   `rms_lf` to dB, `spike_count` to log2. Order matters: the filter then runs in log space,
   which is the right space for quantities that vary multiplicatively across the brain.
2. **Filter.** A total-variation (Chambolle) filter over the probe surface. Each feature is
   interpolated onto a regular grid in `(lateral_um, axial_um)`, filtered, and interpolated
   back. Channels with a non-zero label are dropped and interpolated over rather than
   filtered.

The insight it exploits: neighbouring sites are 20 µm apart on an NP1 probe and largely
sample the same tissue, so a channel departing sharply from its neighbours is more likely
noisy than genuinely different. Total variation is chosen over a smoothing filter because
it preserves edges — and region boundaries are exactly the edges you must not blur away.

`fac` sets the filter strength in median-deviation units; higher denoises harder. It is
set per feature group: `DEFAULT_FAC` is `0.1` for the AP, LF and CSD groups and `3` for
waveforms, chosen by a sweep against region-classification accuracy.

**The waveform remap** (`aggregation.apply_waveform_remap`, since 0.9.0) then replaces the
six raw timing and amplitude waveform columns with four interpretable spike-shape ones —
spike width, pre-depolarisation width, amplitude and peak-to-trough ratio. The six are
redundant, and reparametrising them loses no relative information.

That transform and that remap are the reasons the denoised table is not interchangeable
with the raw one. See [core concepts](concepts.qmd).

## Provenance

Every written feature file carries the package versions and parameters in its pandas
`.attrs`. `get_aggregated_snippets_df` reads those attrs back to build the snippet table
that drives aggregation — so provenance is not merely recorded, it is load-bearing. The
aggregated table of `compute_aggregated_features` carries its own: the snippet windows
(`snippet_windows`), the `features_version` and the ibleatools version and git commit,
which pandas keeps when the table is saved to parquet.

When `skip_saved_computation` reuses a cached family, that file keeps the provenance of the
run that created it. A mixed directory therefore tells the truth about each part
separately.

## Schemas as the contract

Pandera schemas in `ephysatlas.features` declare every feature column with its dtype,
description and unit metadata. `ModelRawFeatures` is the union of all families;
`ModelDenoisedFeatures` is the same with the spike-shape columns in place of the raw
waveform ones.

They are what makes the [feature list reference](../reference/feature-list.qmd) derivable
from code rather than hand-maintained, and validation runs at read time
(`read_features_from_disk(strict=True)`) so a malformed table fails at the boundary instead
of deep inside a model. The reader picks the schema from the columns the table actually
carries, so a denoised table written before the remap still validates.
